translations.text: In the second year of the reign of Ahasuerus the Great, on the first day of the month of Adar and Nisan, which is Igrika [?] and Vardoba, Mordecai had a vision. He was the son of Jair, the grandson of Shimei, who was the child of Kish, of the tribe of Benjamin,
a man who was also in the great captivity,
which Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, carried off with Jehoiachin, king of the Jews.
And this was his vision: behold, there was a voice and the cry of tumult and of thunder, and an earthquake and trembling on the earth.
And behold, two dragons came out in it, both of them ready for battle.
As their voice sounded, everything trembled at the noise of their cry, and every nation bore witness.
It was a day of darkness and gloom, of trembling and battle.
And all the nations were preparing for battle, and they prayed to the Lord.
At the sound of their cry, a small spring became a spring and a great river.
And light and the sun shone out. And the rivers rose up, and their honoured ones were swallowed up.

And when Mordecai got up from his sleep, he thought about it: "What might this vision be, or what is the Lord Almighty preparing to do?" And his vision stayed hidden in his heart, and he searched it out in his heart at all times, so that its interpretation might be revealed to him, until the day.
Mordecai was resting in the outer court of the king with Astai and Tedeute, who were two eunuchs of the king,
and Mordecai heard their plotting and their wickedness, how they were conspiring together against King Ahasuerus to kill him. Mordecai acted wisely about this and exposed their plot.
And when the king questioned both of the eunuchs, Mordecai was found to be truthful, and when the eunuchs confessed, they were put to death.
And King Ahasuerus had this affair of theirs written down, and they also wrote Mordecai into the royal book as a record of what he had said.
And the king ordered that Mordecai be honoured in the king's court, and he gave him authority over all the royal gates, to guard them.

And afterwards the king placed him after Haman, the master of the court, the son of Hammedatha the Macedonian, in the king's presence. From then on Haman looked for an opportunity to do harm to Mordecai and to all his people because of this affair, because Mordecai had told the king about the eunuchs, since they were put to death because of him.
And after this, in the days of the great King Ahasuerus, all the provinces from India to Ethiopia, one hundred and twenty-seven provinces, were subject to him.
And Ahasuerus was established on the thrones of his kingdom.
And the king held a birthday banquet with the princes of his court, and among the Persians and the Arsacids, and the governors of the provinces sat before him.
And for one hundred and eighty days they looked at the wealth and the majesty of the king and the honour of his glory.

When those days were coming to an end, the king held a banquet for everyone in the city of Susa, from the greatest to the least. It lasted seven days, inside the royal palace that he had built as his own residence.

And he spread out for his own dwelling [?] fine linen and scarlet [?], and purple woven cloth embroidered with flowers. And a tent was set up whose cords were scarlet and fine linen; its tips were of silver, and its pillars were overlaid with gold. And there was a couch of gold made with carbuncle and emerald.
And there were golden drinking cups, which he gives from time to time to be taken [?], and royal wine, which the king drinks.
And the drinking was done according to custom; so the king commanded that the wish of every man be carried out.
And Queen Vashti joyfully held a great feast for all the women in the royal palace.
And on the seventh day, when the king had grown merry with wine, the king commanded
his servants to bring in Queen Vashti, so that she would come in and stand before the king at the drinking, wearing only her diadem, in front of all his people.
But Vashti would not do the king's will at the hands of the eunuchs. And when the king perceived that Vashti had scorned his will, the king was greatly grieved and blazed up in wrath and anger.
Then the king said to all the wise men who knew the law and just judgment: "Now what should be done to the queen for this, since she did not see fit to do the king's will?"
And all the rulers of the Persians and the Arsacids stood up before him, those who sat before the king's face and those who sat in the royal palace.
Then Bougaios stood up to make a petition and said: "Queen Vashti has wronged not only the king, but all the rulers of the Persians and the Arsacids.
And her falsehood has spread to all the people, for she scorned your command, the king's.

If it seems right to our lord, and if it is pleasing before your wisdom, write to all the lands and proclaim: Queen Vashti, who scorned your word, the king's, remove her, and put in her place a better one, who will show obedience to your word, the king's; and good will come to all kings.
And from then on all women will honor and exalt their husbands, from the peasant to the rich man."
And the king was satisfied in his heart with this advice and decided the matter as he had advised him.
And so they established a memorial concerning Vashti, recording what she had done to King Ahasuerus.
And then the servants advised the king: "Let us seek out beautiful maidens
and let us hand them over to the eunuch in charge, who is the keeper of the women.
And whichever of them pleases you, the king, appoint her in place of Vashti." And they did just as they had promised.
There was a certain Jewish man in the city of Susa whose name was Mordecai, son of Jair, grandson of Shimei, who was son of Kish, of the tribe of Benjamin.
And he had brought up Esther in the faith, for she was the daughter of his father's brother; and the girl was very beautiful in form and lovely of face.

And they took her and brought her into the king's palace. And when Hegai the eunuch, the keeper of the women, saw her, the girl pleased him more than the other women. And Esther found grace and favor before him, and he took more care of her than of the other women and assigned seven maidens to her as attendants.

And when they brought Esther in before the king, she pleased him greatly. They would bring the girls in at evening and send them out in the morning. And when the king had looked over all those virgins, Esther seemed to him better than the rest. She found grace and favour before him, and he set the queen's diadem on her head.
And the king held Esther's wedding publicly, and he commanded that the others be sent away to their own homes.
And after this the Assyrian king raised Haman, son of Hamadatha the Bougaean, to great honour. He decreed that Haman be exalted [?] and that seats be set for him higher than for all his friends.
For all of them bowed down and fell to the ground before him. But while everyone prostrated themselves before him at the king's command, Mordecai never once prostrated himself before him.
And when the king's servants saw that Mordecai did not bow down to Haman, they said to Mordecai: "Why do you disobey the king and not bow down to Haman?"
He answered them: "I worship God." And they reported this about him to Haman.
And when Haman learned of it, he became enraged at Mordecai and blazed up in wrath against him.

And at that time he was looking for a way to kill Mordecai and all his people in a single day. Haman was eager to do it and kept watch for him in anger, because he was grieved and vexed whenever Mordecai passed before his eyes. And with a deceitful heart he advised the king to do evil to Israel.

And Haman spoke to the king like this: "This people is scattered among us in every place of the kingdom. It is a rebellious and disobedient people with a different law, and they do not obey your law, O king. Their wickedness is known to all nations. They have shown contempt for your command, and this belittles your glory.

If it seems right to you, O king, and this judgment pleases your heart, give this people into my hands to be destroyed. I will put it in writing for you, and I will add ten thousand of my own money to your treasury."
And the king took the ring off his hand, gave it to Haman, and said: "Write to every city and province, and seal it with this royal seal. There is no one who can reverse that seal."

Then the king said to him: "Keep your money for yourself, but destroy that race as you wish." And Haman went in to his idols, to learn from them the day of their death. And the lot fell on the thirteenth day of the month of Igrik [?] and of Vardobisa (May) [?]: the slaughter of all the Jews, from [?] to woman, and the carrying off of their children as plunder.

He hurried and sent the letters out everywhere by means of diaspans [?], with the command written in them: "The great king Ahasuerus, to all the hundred and twenty-seven rulers, princes and sword-bearers from India to Ethiopia. This is what I write:

This race has grown very powerful and has taken hold of the whole land. But I have planned [?] that this authority should be made manifest [?] not by uproar but quietly and gently. So carry out this command, revealing it to no one at all. Then you will live in good order, our land will be at peace, our revenue will be clear and what is owed will be paid in full, the life of the people will be well ordered, and peace will be welcome.
When I asked my counsellors, it was arranged in this way. And since we have been given wisdom and understanding that do not change, and firm faith, and also the lasting continuance of our rule,

Haman has shown us the alien condition of that tribe throughout the whole land: that abominable and unclean people has mixed itself in, and they are opposed to the law of all nations. Because of this they have always had to be divided up here and there and kept under rule, and for this reason they would not submit to any king, and this race was scattered here and there.

For they are always hostile, and at all times their law sets them fighting against other people. They have made themselves strangers, they do not acknowledge our command, they always do evil, and nowhere do they obey the will of our authority.

Now we have sent you this order and have written a letter through Haman, whom I confirmed by letter as our second father. Haman [?] has decreed that they be destroyed, with their wives and children, by the sword of the enemy, mercilessly and without warning, on the eighteenth day of the month of Adar, which is called [?],

to slay all the Jews and heathens and to carry off their children, since they have been unruly from of old. Let them all go down to hell together on one day, so that from then on things may be well ordered and no trouble may come upon us.

And behold, the same order was laid down in Susa. Mordecai learned of this whole matter, and the city of Susa itself was shaken by it. There was great weeping among the Jews and bitterness throughout the land.
Mordecai went into his house, took off his garments, put on sackcloth, and poured ashes over himself,
and he went out into the outer court and stood there, because he was not permitted to enter the royal palace in sackcloth. He called one of the eunuchs, sent him in to Esther, and informed her.
The queen said to him: "Take off the sackcloth and come in." But he would not.

Instead he said: "Tell her this: 'Do not be reluctant to go in before the king. Plead before him for me and for the people. Remember the days of your lowliness, when you were brought up by my hand. Haman the [?] has spoken before the king and decreed death for all of us. Now you too pray to God, and pray to the king and speak to him on our behalf, so that he may deliver us from death.'"
And when he had told her of the distress and anguish of Israel,
she sent word out to him and said this:

"You yourself know better than anyone that if a person goes in to the king without being summoned, and the king does not hold out the golden scepter to them, that person is liable to death. The king has not summoned me at all for thirty days now. How then can I go in unsummoned?"
Mordecai sent word in to her and said:

"Even if you neglect your own people and do not help them, God will still help them and save them, but you and your father's house will perish. And who knows whether it was for times like these that you became queen?"
The queen sent word out and said:

"Have the people offer prayer and supplication to the Lord with one heart, and my servants and I will do the same. Then I will go in to speak to the king. If that is how it must be, so be it, and let me die."
And Mordecai did as Esther had commanded.
Mordecai himself also prayed to the Lord, recalling the Lord's deeds, and said:
"O Lord God, Almighty, you who have authority over all things, in whom there is no change, the salvation of the house of Israel:
for you made the heavens and the earth and all the wonders that are under heaven, and you are Lord over all.

For you know all things, and you know the race of Israel. It was not out of insolence or pride that I refused to bow down to that uncircumcised Haman. They wanted me to do it, as if I should have kissed the toes of his feet in order to humble Israel.
I did this for your sake, so that I would not set anyone above you in glory, Lord, and would not bow down to anyone but you, O True One. Nor will I do it by way of [?].
And now, Lord, you who made a covenant with Abraham, spare your people. They have conspired to destroy us, and they want to blot out and wipe out us, the beginning of your peace [?].
Do not disregard your people, whom you delivered from the land of Egypt.
Hear our prayer and spare your inheritance. Turn our mourning into joy, so that we may live and praise you, and do not silence the mouths of those who sing to you.

Queen Esther also fled to the Lord, distressed and afraid of death. She took off her glorious garments and all the ornaments of her head, and she put on mourning clothes. Instead of fragrant ointment she covered her head with ashes and dung, and she humbled her body greatly. She removed all the ornaments of her joy, and in her lowliness she prayed to the Lord and said:
Lord, our only King, you are a helper. Help me, a lowly woman who has no helper but you, for my distress is in your hands.

I have heard from the books of my fathers that you delivered Israel from all the nations, and their fathers from their fathers [?]. You established their name, Israel, as your inheritance forever, and you did for them as you had told them, and you gave them what they asked of you.
We have sinned before you, and you have given us into the hands of our enemies. If we have glorified their idols anywhere [?], you are righteous, Lord!

There is no counting the great number of our afflictions. They have put their hands in the hands of their idols to overturn the decree of your mouth, to blot out your inheritance, to silence the mouths of those who praise you, and to [?] the glory of your name and of your altar,
and to open the mouths of the enemies to praise their vanities, and to marvel at a king of flesh forever.
Do not give your inheritance, Lord, to your hateful enemies, and do not let them rejoice at our fall. Turn their plans back on themselves, and put to shame those who have plotted evil against us.
Appear to us, Lord, and reveal yourself to us in the time of our distress, and do not destroy us.
Put well-ordered words in my mouth, and make my words pleasing before the lion. Turn his heart to hate the one who fights against us, so that he and his followers come to an end.
But rescue us with your strong hand, and help me.
For the knowledge of all things is in your hands. You know that the touch of the uncircumcised is hateful to me, and I hate the glory of the lawless.
You, Lord, know my distress. This ornament of pride on my head is hateful to me. I do not wear it except on the day I appear in public [?], and I loathe it like the rag of a woman who sits apart.
Your handmaid has never eaten at their table. I have not honoured the king's feast, and I have never drunk the wine of [?] libations.
Your handmaid has taken no joy in the days of my feasting, except in you, O Lord.
And now, O Lord, you who have power over all, hear the voice of those who have no hope. Save us from the hands of those who do us evil, and deliver me from the hand of my terror.
On the third day, when Esther had finished her prayer, she took off her mourning clothes. She put on splendid attire and adorned herself.

She called upon God, who knows all things and is the Saviour, and she took two maids with her. One went in front [?] and screened her form. The other followed her, holding the hems of her garments, and she too screened her beauty.
Her face was cheerful at the meeting, but her heart was in anguish.
She passed through all the doors and went in to the king. The king was sitting on his throne of glory, clothed in splendid attire, all of gold, with a precious carbuncle on his head.

He was very terrifying. When he looked up, his face was like fire from that splendour. He looked at her like a handsome and furious young bull. She was afraid, her face fell for fear, and she hid behind the maid who went before her.
God turned the king's heart, and his anger changed into gentleness. The king rose up in distress and came down from his throne. He took her into his arms, held her, and said to her:
"What is it, Esther? I am your brother. Do not be afraid! You will not die, for our affair is a common one, and there will be no more anger against you. And see, here is the golden sceptre."
He touched her neck with it, kissed her, and said to her: "Tell me, what is it?"
She said to him: "I saw you like an angel of God, and my heart melted because of your glory and your anger, my lord."
Sweat was streaming down her face. The king was shaken, and so were all his servants, and they comforted her.
Then the king said: "What is it, Esther? Tell me, and I will grant it to you, even if you ask for part of my kingdom."
Esther began to speak: "Tomorrow is a great day for me. If it pleases you, O king, come, you and your friend Haman, to the feast that I will prepare for you tomorrow."
Then the king commanded: "Tell Haman, so that we may do as Esther wishes." And the two of them went to the meal that Esther had prepared.

It was a great feast. While they were drinking wine, the king said to Esther: "What is it, Queen Esther? What do you desire, or what do you ask of me? Even if you ask for part of my kingdom, I will grant it to you."
Then Esther said: "My petition and my request is this:

if I have found favour before you, O king, and if it pleases you, O king, grant me my petition. If you grant my request, come, you and Haman, to the meal that I will prepare tomorrow, for tomorrow I will do the same again." The king said to her: "Do as you wish." They told Haman all this, and he was amazed. And the king went in and rested.
Haman went to his house and gathered his friends, his sons and his wife Zeresh (Zosara).
He boasted and said: "Today the queen invited no one else to her feast except the king and me alone, and tomorrow I am invited too."
"But this is a grief to me: when I see Mordecai in the king's court, and he does not bow down to me."

Then his wife Zosara [Zeresh] said to him: "He is of some race of the Jews, and so the king has given you authority to destroy the Jews, and the idols have granted you vengeance on them on the day of their destruction. Order a tree of fifty cubits to be cut, and prepare it. Hang him on that tree; rise early and tell the king about him. And now go and make merry with the king." The advice pleased Haman, and he did so.
God, the Ruler of all, took sleep away from the king that night, and he stayed awake. They summoned the readers, and they read to him from the books of records.

There they found the plot of the eunuchs, concerning which Mordecai had done a good deed for the king. The king turned his mind to it and said: "Mordecai is a faithful man, and he can be trusted as a guardian of my life, for because of him I am alive to this day. Yet today I sit on my thrones, and I have given him nothing, and I have not done him this justice."

Then the king said to his servants: "What shall we do for Mordecai, my savior, for this deed?" When the servants understood, they were envious of him, because the fear of Haman was in their hearts. And the king also perceived it.
When it was dawn, the king asked: "Who is standing outside?"
Haman was found there, for he had risen early to speak to the king, so that he might hang Mordecai up. And the king ordered Haman to be called in.

When he came in, the king said to him: "What should we do for the man whom the king would honor, whose glory the king greatly desires?" And Haman reasoned in his heart: "Whose glory would the king desire but mine?"
Then Haman advised the king about the man whose glory the king desires:
"Let them bring for him royal apparel and the horse of state [literally 'of the diadem' or 'of splendor'] that the king rides.

Let one of the king's honored nobles take it and clothe him with it, mount him on the horse, and lead him around the city. Let heralds go before him and cry out: 'This shall happen to whoever honors the king; it shall be done thus to the one whose glory the king desires.'"

The king commanded him: "Go out quickly, get the horse and the apparel as you said, and go and do so for Mordecai the Jew, who guards these royal gates. Let nothing you have spoken of be lacking for him." When Haman learned that it was not he himself who was to be glorified but Mordecai, his heart was utterly crushed, and his spirit grew faint.

Haman took the apparel and got the horse, and he was deeply ashamed before Mordecai, because that day had been fixed for hanging Mordecai up. He said to Mordecai: "Take off that sackcloth." Mordecai trembled, thinking they were leading him to his death. Weeping, he took off the sackcloth and put on the apparel of glory. But it still seemed strange to Mordecai, he was undone with fear, and his heart was in prayer to the Lord. Haman hurried to mount him on the horse, and Haman led him and proclaimed: "So let it be done to the man who honors the king, whose glory the king desires."
Then Haman went to his house in distress, and Mordecai went to his house rejoicing.
And Haman told his wife the whole matter. His wife said to him in front of his counselors: "The evil you were plotting has fallen on you. Now keep silent, for God does justice."
And while they were still speaking of this, the summoner arrived and hurried him to the meal with the king. Then he cheered up, went to the meal and sat down with them.
And when it was [?] of the meal,

the king said to Esther: "What is the cause of your grief, or what do you ask? I grant you whatever you ask, up to half of my kingdom." And Esther stood anxious about telling him of it, for her enemy was before her eyes, and God gave her counsel in his presence.
And Esther said: "If it seems right to you, O king, and is good justice in your heart, grant me my people at this request of mine, and grant my kindred to my soul.

For I and my kindred have been given up to disgrace, and their children to plunder. And until now I did not wish to tell you, so as not to trouble you, my lord, for behold, that man is sitting here, the one who plotted evil against us."

And at once the king became angry and said: "Who is the one who has dared to humble the glory of the kingdom, and who would despise the fear of you?" And when the queen saw that the king was very angry and raging with hatred, she said: "Do not let your heart be angry, my lord. Even this is enough for me, that I have found comfort from you. Enjoy yourself, O king, and tomorrow I will tell the matter to you, the king." And the king made her swear that she would tell him who it was that had dared this arrogance, and what he had done. And the king promised her on oath to do her will, whatever she might wish.
Then Esther took courage and told him about Haman: "He is your false friend, and that man is utterly wicked."
And the king's heart was greatly angered; he rose up and looked all around. But Haman trembled and fell at the feet of Queen Esther while she was sitting on her couch.

And the king turned back to the banquet, and when he saw him, he said: "Was that sin against me not enough for you, that now you even lay hold of my wife in my presence?" Then he said to his servants: "Kill Haman, and let him live no longer."

And at once they led him out, and one of the servants said to the king: "Behold, there is a beam lying in his courtyard, fifty cubits high, which he had prepared to hang on it Mordecai, who spoke good on your behalf, O king. Now, O king, command that he be hanged on it." And the king said: "Hang him."
And the king took the ring off his hand and said: "Seal his house with this."
And he said to Esther and Mordecai: "He wanted to hang the man who rescued me from the hands of the eunuchs. Did he not know that Esther was related to him on his father's side?"

And the king summoned Mordecai and gave him the whole house of Haman, and said to him: "What do you wish? I will do it for you." And Mordecai said: "That you revoke Haman's letters that were sent out everywhere."

And the king commanded that everything be brought back [?]. And Esther said to the king: "Tomorrow give me my enemies, so that I may slay them with the sword." And Queen Esther spoke to the king about the sons of Haman, asking that they perish together with their mother. And the king said: "Let it be so." And they slew many enemies. And in the city of Susa the king granted the queen the slaughter of those men: "Behold, I have given them over to you, and you have authority to hang them." And they did so.
And he sent out a written decree everywhere, as follows:
The great king Ahasuerus, from India to Ethiopia, to the princes and rulers of the hundred and twenty-seven provinces who are loyal to us:

I greet you. Many times [men have been treated] by ever-beneficent and kind [rulers]. We greatly bestowed honor on him, so that he might become wiser. Not only must the evildoers among those subject to us be sought out, but even among the weak it is impossible [?], those who prosper in good things for themselves alone and strive for evil with schemes,

as though they would find favor: not only that men should perish, but the good work which they could not do [?], that too they cut off along with joy [?]. Those who tyrannized over others were repaid with just judgment, and those against whom they spoke wickedness out of hatred escaped judgment [?].
And often those who, through their authority, gave commands concerning the loyal in favor of the less trustworthy also dared to do it in deed: they made the innocent guilty and even shed blood.
And by evil deeds and lies the death of others was confirmed and decreed, and they took no account of the authority by which we kept our mind blameless.
Now caution is needed, as the word has been given to us, and as we see the conduct of so many in rank and authority, and obedience to the law for those who will come after us,
so that the kingdom may be unshaken and every race may live in peace,
and no one may become a slanderer through deceit, but by meeting face to face they may live in quiet.
For Haman son of Hammedatha, the Bougaean, led us to do what was improper. He became estranged even from the truth and departed from the mind of the Persians.
We exalted him through our kindness, and through us he was considered so beloved by people that we even gave him the title of our father. And everyone bowed down to him, and he sat on the [?] seat.
And in his arrogance he could not bear it. For a long time he was undermining [?] us, and he brought guilt upon souls.
And with much deceit he plotted against our perpetual savior Mordecai and his blameless kinswoman Esther, together with their whole race, and he asked for their destruction.
And in this way he devised a scheme [?] against us as well: through devastation he would remove us from the strength of the Persians, and extend [it] as far as Macedonia.
And the Jews were handed over to death by you as many as three times [?], yet no deceit was found among them; rather, they live righteously under their law,
as children of the only true God, who has guided our kingdom, and their affairs have gone well up to now.

Now do this well, and do not carry out the command of the letters that Haman previously wrote to you. For such a deed he was crucified outside the city of Susa, and he was repaid with judgment according to his deed, which was better than others [?].

Now, behold, this letter has been sent. In every place give the Jews authority over their own law. And may they be strengthened, so that in a time of distress they may be ready to take vengeance. And let the Jews throughout the whole realm be prepared to keep the feast in the twelfth month, Adar, which is the month of Igrik [?].

And glorify its fifteenth day as well, for in those days the Almighty brought about salvation and joy for them. Both now and hereafter, may there be a good life for the Persians too. But as for the evil plotters who have been mentioned, may destruction befall them.

But the cities and villages that do not carry out this command in full [?]: let them be given alive to the fire, and let them be empty not only of people but also of beasts and birds. He confirmed [?]
And this decree was set down in the city of Susa, just as the word of the command had been given there.

And the king also gave Mordecai authority to write wherever he wished. And Mordecai sent out letters and sealed them with the seal of the king's hand. The letters said that his people should stand firm, village by village, and on that day should worship God. And the letter that Mordecai sent read as follows: "Haman, as you know, sent you letters and said that the Jewish people were disobedient: 'Hurry and gather them, send them to me, and I will destroy them.' But I, Mordecai, inform you that the man who made that plot has now been hanged at the gates of the city of Susa. And his house has been given to me, for he wanted to destroy us in the thirteenth month, Adar, which is Igrika [?]."

And Mordecai went out dressed in royal robes. A crown of gold was set on his head, and his diadem was of fine linen and purple. And when the city of Susa saw him, all of it rejoiced. The Hebrews who lived in Susa saw him and rejoiced.
And among the Jews there was light, drinking and joy. They had brightness and delight.

And many of the Jews were circumcised, and from then on no one was hostile to them any longer, because people were afraid of them. And in the cities and villages, wherever the king's command was posted, there was joy, delight and drinking. And many of the gentiles were circumcised and lived as Jews out of fear of the Hebrews.

And from then on the rulers and the officials, the courtiers, the princes and all the scribes honored the Jews, because the fear of Mordecai had fallen on them. For the house of Haman had become guilty [?] in the city of Susa, and the news of his hostility had spread throughout the whole realm.
And in the city of Susa the Jews killed about seven hundred men,
including Pharsan and his brother, and Pharnasar,
and Gaba, and Pardatha,
and Marmesim, and Izadut: the ten sons of Haman, enemies of the Jews.
And they carried off all their goods.
Then the king said to Esther: "What do you wish to be done here? And what should be done in the villages?"
Esther said: "Give the Jews authority to kill whomever they wish and to carry off whatever they find."
And he allowed her this.
And they killed seventy thousand one hundred men.
And Mordecai wrote this account in a letter and sent it to the Jews who lived under the rule of King Ahasuerus, both far and near.
And they established those days, the twelfth and the fifteenth of that month, as days of singing and delight in place of mourning and weeping.
And they sent gifts to the poor, and the poor received them.
For this reason they named these days Purim (Pharaia), because of the lot that fell to them, as a memorial of those days.
And the king sent a written decree imposing a tribute to be remembered, the power of land and sea
and its wealth. And Mordecai was honored, and he wrote it in the book of the Persians and the Arsacids as a memorial.
And Mordecai ruled next after King Ahasuerus, and he became great in royal dignity. He was beloved by all the Jews and esteemed by them, glorious, and a comforter of his people.
And Mordecai said: "All this came from God."
For he remembered the vision he had seen, and it had been fulfilled in deed.
And he said: "The little spring is Esther.
And the two dragons are I and Haman.
And the river is the nations who gathered to destroy the Jews. The sun and the light that was upon the Jews is the help of God. And this is its interpretation."
And God performed this sign and wonder, which had not been done among the nations.
And he divided them into two portions: one for the people of God and one for the nations.
And these two portions were to be for a time and a day of decree forever among all the nations. The Lord remembered his people and vindicated his inheritance.
And all the people cried out with a loud voice and said: "Blessed are you, O Lord, who remembered the covenant of our fathers. Amen!"

Let these days be theirs, in the month of Adar, on the twelfth [?] day, of the fourteenth of that month [?], for assembly, joy, and gladness before God, for the race of the people of Israel forever. Amen!
